place.zh: 石坳村 · 家中 · 天未亮

setup.zh: 立冬这天，天还没亮。娘卸下一条鹿腿，塞进一只小腌菜坛子，往你怀里一塞：「给吴婆婆送一坛腌菜去。走屋后头，趁天没亮。」
setup.en: The Start of Winter, before dawn. Your mother takes off one leg of the deer, stuffs it into a small pickle jar and pushes the jar into your arms: "Take Granny Wu a jar of pickles. Go round the back. Before it's light."

recap.zh: 立冬天没亮，你抱着一坛「腌菜」躲过马家的家丁，给吴婆婆送去了鹿腿。她讲了一个故事：一口鼎，一条龙，一张掉下来的弓——鼎湖，乌号。然后她朝你肩上看不见的银光，慢慢低下了头。
recap.en: Before dawn on the Start of Winter you carried a jar of "pickles" past the Mas' men and brought Granny Wu the leg of venison. She told a story: a *ding*, a dragon, a bow that fell — Dinghu, Wuhao. Then she slowly bowed her head toward the silver on your shoulder she could not see.

zh: 一只腌菜坛子，芥菜底下压着一条鹿腿。
「早年间，有一个皇帝……铸了一口鼎。」
她朝着那团看不见的银光，低下了头。
en: A pickle jar; under the mustard greens, a leg of venison.
"Long ago there was an emperor… he cast a *ding*."
She bows her head toward a silver light she cannot see.

story.zh:
立冬这天，天还没亮，小满是给他娘剁骨头的声音吵醒的。

「咚。咚。咚。」一声一声，又沉又稳。他爬起来往灶间一看，只见他娘挽着袖子，拿他爹那把剥皮的短刀，正在卸那头鹿的一条后腿。她下刀极准，顺着骨缝一刀一刀地走，走到关节那里，手腕一翻，「喀」的一声，一整条后腿便卸了下来，干干净净。他爹蹲在一旁看着，张着嘴，看了半天，道：「……你什么时候学的？」他娘道：「看你剥了十几年兔子。」

她到炕头打开那只木箱，翻出一块包腿的布来。翻的时候，她把箱底一个巴掌大的旧布包拿起来，搁在一边；找着了布，又把那个布包放回了原处，放得很轻，轻得像放一个睡着了的孩子。小满知道那布包里包的是什么，那是那只碗的七八片。

她在膝弯那里又下了一刀，把鹿腿斩作两截，拿布包了，揭开墙角那只腌菜缸——缸不大，口有脸盆宽，是腌芥菜疙瘩的——把上面一层芥菜扒开，把两截鹿腿塞了进去，又把芥菜扒回来，一层一层压实了，盖上木盖。小满道：「娘，鹿腿也能腌？」他娘道：「能。」小满道：「好吃吗？」他娘道：「不知道。没腌过。」说着拿草绳把那只缸捆了，往他背上一绑，道：「给吴婆婆送一缸腌菜去。走屋后头，别走井台。趁天没亮。」

小满背着缸，一肚子的不明白。他娘却已把剩下的肉、皮、角、下水，都在院子里摊开了，摊得整整齐齐，像是摆摊，那一挂下水，偏偏摆在最当门的地方。然后她洗了手，把袖子放下来，坐在门槛里头，等着。小满出门时回头看了一眼，想起说书先生讲的姜太公钓鱼，钩是直的；他娘这一钩，挂的是一挂下水。
story.en:
On the Start of Winter, before it was light, Xiaoman was woken by the sound of his mother chopping bone.

*Thok. Thok. Thok.* One stroke after another, heavy and steady. He got up and looked into the kitchen: his mother, sleeves rolled, was taking one hind leg off the deer with his father's skinning knife. She cut very true, working along the seam of the bone stroke by stroke; at the joint she turned her wrist — *crack* — and the whole hind leg came away, clean. His father crouched to one side watching, mouth open, a long while. "…When did you learn that?" His mother said, "Watching you skin rabbits for ten-odd years."

She opened the wooden chest at the head of the kang and dug out a cloth to wrap the leg. As she searched, she lifted a small old cloth bundle, the size of a palm, from the bottom of the chest and set it aside; when she had found the cloth she put the bundle back where it had been, very gently, as gently as laying down a sleeping child. Xiaoman knew what was wrapped in it: the seven or eight pieces of that bowl.

She cut once more, at the hock, so the leg came apart in two pieces, wrapped them in the cloth, and took the wooden lid off the pickle crock in the corner — not a big crock, its mouth as wide as a washbasin, the one for mustard tubers. She pushed aside the top layer of greens, stuffed the two pieces in, pushed the greens back over it, pressed them down layer by layer, and put the lid on. Xiaoman said, "Ma, can you pickle a deer leg?" His mother said, "You can." Xiaoman said, "Is it good?" His mother said, "Don't know. Never pickled one." And she roped the crock and tied it onto his back. "Take Granny Wu a crock of pickles. Go round the back of the houses, not by the well. Before it gets light."

Xiaoman stood with the crock on his back and a bellyful of not understanding. His mother had already laid out the rest — meat, hide, antlers, offal — all over the yard, neat and orderly, like a market stall, and the offal she set right in front of the door. Then she washed her hands, let down her sleeves, sat down just inside the threshold, and waited. On his way out Xiaoman looked back once and remembered the storyteller's Jiang Taigong fishing with a straight hook; his mother's hook had a set of offal hung on it.

story.zh:
天刚蒙蒙亮，小满背着缸，贴着各家的后墙根走，在老刘家屋后迎面撞上了两个马家的家丁。提灯笼的揭开缸盖，把手伸进芥菜堆里掏了两把，掏出来一手的咸水，一根芥菜疙瘩——再往下一拃，就摸着了。

小满道，是给村东头吴婆婆送的。石坳村的人，谁都不大愿意去村东头那个门槛跟前，马家的家丁也一样，摆了摆手：「去去去。」小满背着缸走出去十几步，才觉出后背上的汗，已经把衣裳贴住了。

村东头那户，吴婆婆已经坐在门槛上了，脸朝着东边，那里刚刚透出一线鱼肚白，她晒的大约是这一线白。

小满走到她跟前，还没开口，她已道：「鹿腿来了？」

小满背着缸，愣住了。他娘一个字也没提鹿腿，那两个家丁凑着鼻子也没闻出来。他道：「……您怎么知道是鹿腿？」

吴婆婆道：「你爹答应的。在山涧边上，蹲着摸那个蹄印的时候。」

小满心里「咯噔」一下。那山涧在黑松岭里头，离这门槛少说也有三四十里地，隔着断碑，隔着一整座岭子。他道：「婆婆，您又不在山涧边上。」

吴婆婆笑了，露出那三颗牙来：「我耳朵好。」

她等小满把缸卸下来，揭开盖子闻了闻，道：「你娘是个聪明人。」说着拍了拍门槛，道：「坐。」

小满便坐下了，心里记着他娘的话：老人家说话，十句里有九句是废话，剩下那一句，能救命。

她先说她那三颗牙，说是在等什么东西，等到了，才肯掉。小满问等什么，她说不知道，牙没说。

说完了牙，她道：「你爷爷那张弓，昨儿拉开了？」小满又是一愣，道：「……拉开了。」吴婆婆点了点头，道：「我给你讲个故事罢。」

她仰着脸，朝着东边那一线白，慢慢地道：「早年间，有一个皇帝。这皇帝，是天底下头一个皇帝，比马家老爷大，比县太爷大，比县太爷的县太爷还大。他采了山上的铜，在一座山底下，铸了一口鼎。」

小满道：「鼎是什么？」

吴婆婆道：「一口大锅。」

小满道：「皇帝铸一口锅做什么？」

吴婆婆道：「煮饭。」

小满觉得这个答法很有道理，便不再问了。

吴婆婆道：「那口鼎铸成的那一天，天上下来一条龙。那龙从云里垂下它的胡须来，胡须一直垂到地上，是来接那皇帝上天的。皇帝便骑上去了。跟着他的大官，他的娘娘，一个一个也都爬上去了，爬上去七十几个。龙便往天上飞。」

她顿了一顿，声音慢了下来：「剩下的是些小官儿，官儿小，挤不上去。有一个小官儿，官小得连名字都没人记得，他家就在那山脚底下，家里有个闺女，才七八岁。他不甘心，扑上去抓住了龙的胡须，死死地抓着，吊在半空里，底下他闺女仰着脸，一声一声地喊他。那胡须哪里吃得住这许多人？扯断了。人都掉了下来。跟着掉下来的，还有那皇帝的一张弓。」

小满的心，不知怎的，忽然跳快了一下。

他道：「那闺女呢？」吴婆婆道：「……哭呗。」

她停了一停，又道：「底下的老百姓，仰着头，看着那皇帝上了天，一个一个，都抱着那张弓，抱着那一把扯断的龙须，哭。后来的人，便管那个地方叫鼎湖，管那张弓，叫乌号。上去的上去了，留下的，就守着一张弓。」小满等了一会儿，问道：「那张弓，后来有人拉开过吗？」

吴婆婆转过脸来，朝着他，那张满是皱纹的脸上，慢慢地露出一个笑来。她道：「你问得好。」

她只说了这四个字，便不再往下说了。

小满又等了一会儿，道：「婆婆，这故事是您编的吧？」吴婆婆道：「不是。一个皇帝，讲给另一个皇帝听的。后头那个皇帝听完了，说：我要是能像前头那个一样上天，扔下老婆孩子，就跟脱一只鞋一样。」

小满皱起眉头：「那他上去了吗？」

吴婆婆道：「没有。」

顿了一顿，又自言自语地添了一句：「修仙修仙，修了一辈子，修成个想上天的人，也就修到头了。剩下那一句，就是这个。」

说完了，她又伸出那只枯瘦的手来，摸了摸小满的头，又摸了摸他的肩膀，摸到了他脖子上那条「围脖」，她的手便停住了。

她的手停在那团银毛上，一动也不动，好像生怕一动，便会把什么东西惊醒了。

然后，她把手收了回去。她朝着那团谁都看不见的银光，很慢、很慢地，低下了头。她的腰本来就弯，这一低，头几乎低到了膝盖上。她低着头，低了一会儿，又慢慢地抬起来，脸上什么表情也没有，像是方才只是打了个盹。

小满坐在门槛上，一动也不敢动，想问，又不知道该问谁。吴婆婆道：「回罢。日头上来了，马家的人，也该到了。」
story.en:
Day was just breaking. Xiaoman, the crock on his back, went along the back walls of the houses, and behind old Liu's house he ran straight into two Ma servants. The one with the lantern took off the lid, put his hand into the greens, dug twice, and came out with a fistful of brine and one mustard tuber — one more hand-span down and he'd have touched it.

Xiaoman said it was for Granny Wu at the east end. Nobody in Shi'ao Village much liked going up to that threshold at the east end, and the Ma servants were no different; they waved him off: "Go on, go on." Xiaoman walked a dozen paces with the crock before he felt the sweat that had glued his shirt to his back.

At the house at the east end, Granny Wu was already sitting on her threshold, face turned east, where the first fish-belly white was just showing; it was probably that strip of white she was sunning in.

Xiaoman came up to her, and before he spoke she said, "The venison's come?"

Xiaoman stood with the crock on his back, stunned. His mother hadn't said a word about a deer leg, and those two servants with their noses in it hadn't smelled it. He said, "…How do you know it's a deer leg?"

Granny Wu said, "Your father promised. By the mountain stream, crouched there feeling the hoofprint."

Xiaoman's heart gave a jolt. That stream was inside Black Pine Ridge, thirty or forty li from this threshold at least, past the stele, past a whole ridge. "Granny, you weren't by the stream."

Granny Wu laughed, showing her three teeth. "My ears are good."

She waited for Xiaoman to set the crock down, then lifted the lid and sniffed. "Your mother is a clever woman." She patted the threshold. "Sit."

So Xiaoman sat, remembering what his mother said: of every ten things old folk say, nine are nonsense, and the one left over can save your life.

First she talked about her three teeth: they were waiting for something, she said, and only when it came would they fall. Xiaoman asked what they were waiting for. She said she didn't know; the teeth hadn't said.

When she'd finished with her teeth, she said, "Your grandpa's bow — you drew it yesterday?" Xiaoman was stunned again. "…I drew it." Granny Wu nodded. "Let me tell you a story."

She lifted her face toward that strip of white in the east and said slowly: "Long ago there was an emperor. This emperor was the very first emperor under heaven — bigger than old Master Ma, bigger than the county magistrate, bigger than the county magistrate's county magistrate. He took copper from the mountain, and at the foot of a mountain he cast a *ding*."

Xiaoman said, "What's a *ding*?"

Granny Wu said, "A big pot."

Xiaoman said, "Why would an emperor cast a pot?"

Granny Wu said, "To cook rice."

Xiaoman found this a very reasonable answer and asked no more.

Granny Wu said, "The day that *ding* was cast, a dragon came down from the sky. The dragon let its whiskers down out of the clouds, whiskers that reached right to the ground — come to take the emperor up to heaven. So the emperor climbed on. His great officers, his consorts, climbed up after him one by one, seventy-odd of them. And the dragon flew up toward heaven."

She paused, and her voice slowed: "The ones left were small officials; too small to squeeze on. There was one of them, so small nobody even remembers his name, whose home was right at the foot of that mountain, and he had a daughter, seven or eight years old. He wouldn't give up; he threw himself at it and grabbed the dragon's whiskers, clung on for dear life, hanging in mid-air, and below him his daughter turned up her face and called him, again and again. How could the whiskers hold so many? They tore. The people all fell. And down with them fell the emperor's bow."

Xiaoman's heart, somehow, beat faster for a moment.

He said, "And the daughter?" Granny Wu said, "…Cried, what else."

She paused, then went on: "The common folk below looked up and watched the emperor go up into heaven, and one and all they hugged that bow, hugged that handful of snapped dragon whiskers, and wept. Later people called that place Dinghu, and that bow, Wuhao. Those who went up went up; those left behind kept a bow." Xiaoman waited a while, then asked: "That bow — did anyone ever draw it after?"

Granny Wu turned her face to him, and on that face full of wrinkles a smile came slowly. She said, "You ask well."

She said only those three words, and went no further.

Xiaoman waited again, then said, "Granny, you made this story up, didn't you?" Granny Wu said, "No. One emperor told it to another emperor. When the second emperor heard it, he said: if I could go up to heaven like the first one, I'd leave my wife and children as easily as kicking off a shoe."

Xiaoman frowned. "Did he go up?"

Granny Wu said, "No."

After a pause she added, half to herself: "Cultivating immortality, cultivating immortality — cultivate a whole lifetime, and if what you've cultivated is a man who wants to go up to heaven, that's as far as it goes. That's the one left over."

When she'd finished, she reached out her bony hand again, touched Xiaoman's head, then his shoulder, and found the "scarf" round his neck, and there her hand stopped.

Her hand rested on that silver fur, not moving at all, as though afraid that any movement would wake something.

Then she drew her hand back. Toward that silver light nobody could see, very, very slowly, she bowed her head. Her back was bent to begin with; bowed like this, her head went nearly to her knees. She stayed bowed a while, then slowly straightened, her face showing nothing, as though she'd only nodded off.

Xiaoman sat on the threshold and didn't dare move; he wanted to ask, and didn't know whom to ask. Granny Wu said, "Go home. The sun's up; the Mas will be on their way."

label.en: Stay in and watch over it

exits.means: stays home with the fox that night

story.zh:
那缸腌菜，是他爹送去的。他爹瘸着腿去了，瘸着腿回来，说吴婆婆接了缸，揭开盖子闻了闻，什么也没说，只朝着他们家这边，坐了好一会儿。

小满没出门。他守着怀里那团凉冰冰的银毛，数了三遍它还在不在喘气。日头上来了，马家的人，也该到了。
story.en:
It was his father who took the crock over. He limped there and limped back, and said Granny Wu took the crock, lifted the lid and sniffed, and said not a word, only sat facing their house for a good while.

Xiaoman stayed in. He watched over the cold silver fur inside his jacket, and three times counted whether it was still breathing. The sun was up; the Mas would be coming.
